english.html: to flee <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>; and although Saint Paul burned with a continual desire and ardent zeal to attain to the heavenly inheritance, and to be separated from the body, to dwell with Jesus Christ <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>: nevertheless, to wish at certain times, and for some vexation that befalls, for the last sigh and period of one's life, is the speech of a person too much subject to her passions, and, for the rest, ill instructed in the law of God; of whom, being his vassals and most bounden servants, we must wait upon all his commandments. And, as Hegesippus said, we must not wish to depart from this world sooner, nor to remain in it longer, than the good God who has given us being and life wills and commands it. And it is not lawful to cut the thread of life, or to dissolve the soul from the body, for any other than him who joined it. And just as Plato says that those who by authority of the magistrate are made prisoners must not go out of the prison before the magistrate by whose authority they were put in orders it, so neither must we, without the will of the Lord God who has given us the soul, drive it from us, draw it out, or put it forth from the prison of this mortal and miserable body <sup class="mk" data-key="c2">c2</sup>. Saint Augustine in a certain place occupies and labours himself greatly to show the great fault committed by those who desire, and still worse those who execute, a voluntary death upon their own persons, singularly when they do it for fear of punishment or of infamy <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. Which before him Aristotle had learnedly discoursed, saying that it is not the act of a constant and virtuous man, but rather of a timid and cowardly one, to slay oneself with one's own hands, and to make oneself the cruel minister of one's own death, in order to flee punishment, poverty, or some other discontent <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. I know well that in time past Hannibal, Cato, Cassius, Brutus, Nero, Diocletian, Sardanapalus, Cleopatra, and several others, so as not to fall into the hands of their enemies, killed themselves, or had themselves killed by their servants. And others have done no less from an impatience of grief, wearied by the martyrdom of some sad and lamentable passion <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>: as the Emperor Hadrian, and Silius Italicus, an excellent poet, both overcome by incredible torments of sickness; as

notes.citation: Cicero, Letters to his Friends 11.28.2, the letter of C. Matius to Cicero: numquam enim honestam mortem fugiendam, saepe etiam oppetendam putavi; Coras's "Numantius" is a slip or a wrong sort for Matius
notes.original: Ciceron au liure xi. deſd. epiſtres.

notes.citation: Philippians 1 (1:23: "having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ")

notes.gloss: Socrates: a man must not take his own life until God sends some necessity, as now to me; we are in a kind of guard-post (φρουρά), and the gods are our keepers. Coras turns the image into the prisoner who may not leave the magistrate's prison unbidden. The note is printed with the key c, repeating the key of the previous note; the transcription gives it c2.

notes.citation: Augustine, The City of God, book I, chapters 17 to 28 (1.17–27 treat suicide: the Christian women who killed themselves to escape rape, Lucretia, Cato, and the rule that no one may kill himself to avoid another's sin or his own shame)
notes.original: S-Auguſtin au i. liure de ciuita. Dei c. xvij. inſque au xxviij.
notes.gloss: The Loys Viues of the case file §7 is the commentator on this book; Coras here cites Augustine himself.

notes.citation: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book IV chapter 7 as printed; the passage is III.7 (1116a12–15): to die to escape poverty or love or anything painful is the mark not of a brave man but of a coward (cf. V.11, 1138a, on the suicide's injustice to the city)
notes.original: Ariſtote au iiij. des Ethiques c. vij.

notes.citation: Digest 48.21.3 (De bonis eorum qui ante sententiam vel mortem sibi consciverunt vel accusatorem corruperunt, l. 3, Marcian)
notes.original: l. iii. D. de bon. eo. qui mort. ſibi cõſ.
notes.gloss: Those who kill themselves taedio vitae vel impatientia doloris aut iactationis — "from weariness of life or impatience of pain or from vainglory" — keep their testament and their goods pass to their heirs, as against those who die to escape a pending charge; Coras's impatience de douleur is the law's phrase.
